Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- Coalition troops on Monday formally handed over security control of Iraq's Anbar province -- once the hub of the country's Sunni insurgency, to Iraqis on Monday. A U.S. soldier on patrol in Ramadi's market earlier this year. U.S. troops will remain in the province to support Iraqi forces. President George W. Bush described the transfer as a major victory against al-Qaeda extremists who once held sway in the area. "Today, Anbar is no longer lost to al Qaeda -- it is al Qaeda that lost Anbar," he said in a statement. Once dominated by Sunni insurgents, Anbar has been the scene of many attacks on U.S.-led troops in Iraq. Now a bastion of tribal opposition, it is also the scene of an internal Sunni political struggle between the Iraqi Islamic Party, one of Iraq's main Sunni parties, and the Awakening movement, the first anti-al Qaeda in Iraq movement established in the country. More than 25,000 U.S. troops serve in the sprawling Anbar province west of Baghdad; most of them Marines. They will remain for the time being but will shift their mission to supporting Iraqi forces, when needed . The transfer is a "major progress" for all of Iraq, said Brigadier Gen. David Perkins, the spokesman for the Multi-National Force in Iraq. The transfer ceremony took place in Ramadi, the capital of the western province, and was attended by Iraqi officials and U.S. military brass.  Watch U.S., Iraqi officials perform transfer » . "We are all well aware of what the security situation was in Anbar even a year ago," Perkins said. "And the fact that that has been able to be turned around, that the Iraqi citizens that live there want to stand up on their own, [that] they want to take control of the province on their own ... it's a major progress not only for Anbar, but for all of Iraq." Anbar is the 11th of Iraq's 18 provinces to revert to local security control, but is the first Sunni-dominated one. The move comes amid a big drop in violence in Iraq and calls from Iraqis for the United States to come up with a troop withdrawal timetable. The other provinces that have transitioned to Iraqi security control are Duhuk, Irbil and Sulaimaniya in the Kurdish region, and Karbala, Najaf, Qadisiya, Muthanna, Thiqar, Basra, and Maysan in the Shiite south. CNN's Jomana Karadsheh and Arwa Damon in Baghdad contributed to this report.

BAGHDAD, Iraq (CNN) -- On Monday, coalition forces officially transferred responsibility for securing Iraq's Anbar province—formerly the center of the nation's Sunni insurgency—into Iraqi hands. Although American troops will stay in the region, their role will shift to backing up Iraqi security forces.

President George W. Bush characterized the handover as a significant triumph over al-Qaeda extremists who previously dominated the area. "Today, Anbar is no longer lost to al Qaeda -- it is al Qaeda that lost Anbar," he stated in a written release.

Anbar, previously under the control of Sunni insurgents, has witnessed numerous assaults on U.S.-led forces throughout the Iraq conflict. Today it stands as a stronghold of tribal resistance, while also serving as the battleground for a Sunni political rivalry between the Iraqi Islamic Party—among Iraq's leading Sunni political groups—and the Awakening movement, which was the first organization in the country to oppose al-Qaeda in Iraq.

Over 25,000 American service members, the majority of them Marines, are stationed across the vast Anbar province situated west of the capital. For now, these forces will stay in place, though their responsibilities will change toward assisting Iraqi troops whenever the need arises.

According to Brigadier Gen. David Perkins, who serves as spokesman for the Multi-National Force in Iraq, the handover represents "major progress" for the entire nation. The ceremony marking the transition was held in Ramadi, the provincial capital, with both Iraqi authorities and senior U.S. military commanders in attendance.

"We are all well aware of what the security situation was in Anbar even a year ago," Perkins remarked. "And the fact that that has been able to be turned around, that the Iraqi citizens that live there want to stand up on their own, [that] they want to take control of the province on their own ... it's a major progress not only for Anbar, but for all of Iraq."

Out of Iraq's 18 provinces, Anbar becomes the 11th to return to local security oversight, yet it is the first among those with a Sunni majority to do so. This development occurs against a backdrop of significantly reduced violence across Iraq, along with growing Iraqi demands that Washington establish a schedule for pulling out its forces.

The provinces already placed under Iraqi security authority include Duhuk, Irbil, and Sulaimaniya within the Kurdish territory, plus Karbala, Najaf, Qadisiya, Muthanna, Thiqar, Basra, and Maysan throughout the Shiite south.

CNN's Jomana Karadsheh and Arwa Damon in Baghdad contributed to this report.

# Coalition Forces Transfer Security Control of Anbar Province to Iraqi Authorities

In a landmark moment for Iraq's ongoing stabilization efforts, coalition troops formally handed over security control of the country's Anbar province to Iraqi forces. The transfer marked a significant milestone, as Anbar became the first Sunni-dominated province to revert to local Iraqi control—a symbolic and strategic achievement in the broader campaign to restore self-governance across the nation.

President George W. Bush hailed the transfer as a major victory against al-Qaeda extremists. In his remarks, he emphasized the significance of the achievement, declaring that "it is al Qaeda that lost Anbar." The President's statement underscored the dramatic shift in the region's fortunes and the diminishing influence of extremist groups that had once operated freely within the province.

The transformation of Anbar has been remarkable. Once the hub of Iraq's Sunni insurgency and the site of numerous deadly attacks on U.S.-led troops, the province has evolved into a bastion of tribal opposition to al-Qaeda. Local tribal leaders, who had previously either tolerated or actively supported insurgent activities, turned decisively against the extremists, playing a crucial role in reclaiming their communities and restoring order.

Despite the handover of security responsibilities, the American military presence in Anbar will not disappear entirely. More than 25,000 U.S. troops, the majority of them Marines, will remain stationed in the province. However, their mission will shift fundamentally—from leading security operations to supporting Iraqi forces when their assistance is needed. This adjustment reflects the growing capability and confidence of Iraqi security personnel to manage their own affairs.

According to Brigadier General David Perkins, the handover reflects a significant drop in violence across Iraq. He characterized the transfer as representing major progress not only for Anbar itself but for the entire country. The successful transition of such a strategically important and previously volatile province stands as a testament to the improving security environment and offers hope for the continued stabilization of Iraq as a whole.

# Security Control of Anbar Province Transferred to Iraqi Forces

In a significant milestone marking Iraq's ongoing progress toward stability and self-governance, Coalition troops formally transferred security control of Anbar province to Iraqi forces. The handover represents a dramatic turnaround for a region that was once considered the epicenter of Iraq's Sunni insurgency and a primary stronghold for al-Qaeda activity.

Anbar, Iraq's largest province by area, had for years been synonymous with some of the most intense and deadly fighting of the conflict. The vast western region, which shares borders with Syria, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia, had witnessed brutal violence and served as a critical base of operations for extremist groups seeking to destabilize the country.

While the transfer places security responsibilities in the hands of Iraqi forces, the transition does not signal a complete withdrawal of American presence. More than 25,000 U.S. troops will remain stationed in the province, prepared to provide support and assistance to their Iraqi counterparts when needed. This arrangement reflects a gradual, measured approach to the handover, ensuring that local forces are not left without backup as they assume greater control.

The significance of this transfer extends beyond Anbar's borders. It marks the first Sunni-dominated province to revert to local Iraqi control, and the eleventh province overall to make this transition. The handover comes amid a substantial and sustained decrease in violence throughout the region—a development that officials have hailed as evidence of major progress.

Military and government officials characterized the transfer as a meaningful victory against al-Qaeda extremists, whose influence in the area had been significantly diminished. More broadly, the milestone was described as an encouraging sign of forward momentum for Iraq as a whole, suggesting that the country was moving steadily toward the goal of managing its own security affairs and building a more stable future.

# Coalition Forces Transfer Security Control of Anbar Province to Iraqi Authorities

**Once the deadliest region in Iraq, Anbar becomes 11th of 18 provinces handed to Iraqi control**

Coalition forces formally transferred security responsibility for Iraq's western Anbar province to Iraqi authorities on Monday, marking a significant milestone in the country's efforts to assume control over its own security.

The handover ceremony, held at a government facility in the provincial capital of Ramadi, was attended by Iraqi and coalition military officials, tribal leaders, and provincial government representatives. The transfer makes Anbar the 11th of Iraq's 18 provinces to return to Iraqi security control.

"This is a proud day for Iraq and a testament to the courage and sacrifice of our forces," an Iraqi government official said during the ceremony. "The people of Anbar have shown that stability is possible."

## A Dramatic Turnaround

The transfer represents a remarkable reversal for a province that was once considered among the most violent and dangerous in Iraq. Anbar, a vast desert region stretching to the borders of Syria, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia, had for years been a stronghold for insurgents and a center of sectarian violence.

The security situation began to shift when local Sunni tribal leaders turned against extremist elements, forming alliances with coalition forces in what became known as the "Awakening" movement. This grassroots effort, combined with the deployment of additional troops, contributed to a substantial decline in violence across the province.

## Ongoing Responsibilities

Under the terms of the transfer, Iraqi army and police units now hold primary responsibility for maintaining security in Anbar. Coalition forces will remain available to provide support and assistance if requested by Iraqi commanders but will shift to an overwatch role.

Military officials cautioned that challenges remain and that the security gains, while significant, are not irreversible. They emphasized the importance of continued economic development, reconstruction, and political reconciliation to sustain the progress achieved.

## Looking Ahead

The handover comes as officials continue to work toward transferring the remaining provinces to Iraqi control. The progress in Anbar has been cited by military leaders as evidence that Iraqi forces are increasingly capable of managing their own security responsibilities.

Local residents expressed cautious optimism about the transfer, with many hoping it signals a lasting return to normalcy after years of conflict.

*This is a developing story and will be updated.*

# Iraqi Forces Take Control of Anbar Province in Milestone Handover

**BAGHDAD** — Iraqi security forces formally assumed control of Anbar province on Monday, marking a significant turning point in a region that was once the deadliest battleground for American troops and the heart of the Sunni insurgency.

The handover ceremony, held in the provincial capital of Ramadi, transferred responsibility for security in the sprawling western desert province from U.S. forces to the Iraqi army and police. Anbar becomes the 11th of Iraq's 18 provinces to revert to Iraqi control, but it carries a symbolic weight far exceeding the others.

"This is a great day for Iraq," said a senior Iraqi official at the ceremony, where American and Iraqi flags flapped in the desert heat and helicopters circled overhead. "Anbar was written off as lost, and today it is returned to its people."

Just two years ago, a U.S. Marine intelligence report famously concluded that the province was all but lost to al-Qaeda in Iraq. Ramadi and Fallujah were synonymous with roadside bombs, suicide attacks and some of the most intense urban combat of the war.

The dramatic reversal is credited largely to the "Awakening" movement, in which Sunni tribal sheiks turned against al-Qaeda militants and aligned themselves with American forces beginning in late 2006. That shift, combined with the influx of additional U.S. troops in the 2007 "surge," helped drive violence in the province to a fraction of its former levels.

Marine commanders point to the numbers: attacks that once totaled hundreds per week across Anbar have fallen to a handful. Markets have reopened in Fallujah and Ramadi, and reconstruction projects have begun in cities that were largely reduced to rubble.

Still, officials on both sides cautioned that security remains fragile. The province has seen a series of suicide bombings in recent months, and questions persist over whether the tens of thousands of mostly Sunni Awakening fighters will be integrated into Iraq's Shiite-led security forces or left disaffected and unemployed.

More than 1,000 American service members have died in Anbar since the 2003 invasion, making it among the most costly provinces of the war for U.S. forces.

The Marines are not leaving entirely. American troops will remain in a support and backup role, ready to assist Iraqi units if requested, but Iraqi forces will now lead operations across the province.

For the tribal leaders who gambled their lives on turning against the insurgency, Monday's ceremony represented a hard-won validation.

"We paid for this in blood," one sheik said. "Now the responsibility is ours to keep."

# Anbar Province Returns to Iraqi Control: A Milestone in Security Transition

**RAMADI, Iraq** — In a significant development for Iraq's security landscape, Anbar province formally transferred to Iraqi security control, marking the first Sunni-dominated province to be returned from coalition oversight to full Iraqi authority. The handover represents a notable shift in a region that had once been among the most violent and contested areas of the country.

## A Dramatic Turnaround

Anbar, Iraq's largest province geographically, stretching from the outskirts of Baghdad to the borders of Syria, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia, had been an epicenter of the insurgency in the years following the 2003 invasion. Cities such as Fallujah and Ramadi became synonymous with intense fighting and served as strongholds for al-Qaeda in Iraq and affiliated militant groups.

The transformation of the province from a hotbed of violence to a region deemed stable enough for Iraqi control stands as one of the more remarkable reversals of the conflict.

## The Role of the Awakening Movement

Central to Anbar's turnaround was the emergence of the Sunni "Awakening" movement, known in Arabic as the Sahwa. Beginning around 2006, local Sunni tribal leaders, frustrated by the brutality and heavy-handed tactics of al-Qaeda in Iraq, began organizing against the extremists who had once operated freely in their communities.

These tribal fighters, many of whom had previously fought against coalition forces, allied with U.S. and Iraqi forces to expel militants from their towns and villages. The Awakening councils provided crucial local intelligence, manpower, and legitimacy in the fight against insurgents.

The movement proved instrumental in reducing violence dramatically across the province. However, the integration of Awakening fighters into official Iraqi security structures and government employment remained a delicate and unresolved challenge, raising questions about long-term stability should these fighters feel marginalized by the Shiite-led central government.

## Troop Levels and Security Considerations

At the height of operations in Anbar, tens of thousands of U.S. Marines and soldiers were deployed throughout the province to combat the insurgency. The security improvements allowed for a gradual drawdown of forces in the region as conditions stabilized.

With the handover, responsibility for security across Anbar shifted to Iraqi army and police forces, though coalition troops remained available to provide support and assistance if requested by Iraqi authorities. The transition reflected growing confidence in the capabilities of Iraqi security forces to maintain order independently.

## Sectarian Significance

The return of Anbar carried particular symbolic weight due to its Sunni Arab majority. Previous provincial transfers had occurred primarily in Shiite-majority or Kurdish regions. The successful handover of a Sunni heartland demonstrated that security gains were not confined to areas aligned with the Shiite-dominated central government.

Officials expressed hope that the transfer would help bridge sectarian divisions and encourage greater Sunni participation in Iraq's political process, which many Sunnis had previously boycotted or viewed with suspicion.

## Looking Ahead

While the handover was celebrated as a significant achievement, observers cautioned that challenges remained. The reintegration of Awakening fighters, the distribution of political power, and the equitable delivery of government services and reconstruction funds would all be critical to sustaining the fragile peace.

The transfer of Anbar nonetheless stood as evidence that even Iraq's most troubled regions could achieve meaningful stability, offering a template for security transitions across the country.

---

*This article provides an overview of the security transition in Anbar province and the factors contributing to its stabilization.*

# US Forces Transfer Security Control of Anbar Province to Iraqi Authorities

**RAMADI, Iraq** — American military commanders formally handed control of Anbar province to Iraqi security forces on Monday, marking a significant milestone in the transition of security responsibilities to Baghdad's government in what was once the deadliest region for US troops.

The ceremony, held at a government compound in the provincial capital of Ramadi, brought together Iraqi and American officials to commemorate the transfer of the sprawling western desert province, which shares borders with Syria, Jordan, and Saudi Arabia.

## A Symbolic Turning Point

Anbar became the latest of Iraq's 18 provinces to move to Iraqi security control, and its handover carried particular weight given the region's history. The vast Sunni-majority province was for years the epicenter of the insurgency and a stronghold for al-Qaeda in Iraq, with cities like Fallujah and Ramadi becoming synonymous with some of the fiercest fighting of the war.

The security situation in Anbar improved dramatically following the emergence of the "Awakening" movement, in which local Sunni tribal leaders turned against al-Qaeda militants and aligned with US and Iraqi forces.

## Reactions

Iraqi officials framed the transfer as evidence of the country's growing capacity to manage its own affairs.

"This is a proud day for Anbar and for all of Iraq," a provincial official said at the ceremony, expressing confidence that Iraqi police and army units were prepared to shoulder the responsibility.

American commanders praised the transformation of the province while cautioning that challenges remained.

"The progress here has been remarkable, but this transition reflects hard-won gains that must be protected," a senior US officer noted, emphasizing that American forces would remain available to support Iraqi units when requested.

Local tribal leaders, whose cooperation proved pivotal to reversing the security situation, welcomed the handover while pressing for continued investment in reconstruction and jobs.

## Context and Broader Transition

The transfer is part of a phased, province-by-province process under which Iraqi forces assume the lead role in security, with US troops shifting to a supporting and advisory posture. Under the arrangement, American forces do not withdraw immediately but instead pull back from day-to-day operations, remaining on call to assist when Iraqi authorities ask for help.

Officials stressed that the handover does not signal an end to threats in the province. Sporadic attacks have continued, and observers have warned that unemployment, slow reconstruction, and unresolved political tensions could undermine fragile security gains if left unaddressed.

The completion of the Anbar transfer moves Iraq closer to full sovereign control over its territory, a benchmark closely watched by both governments as they negotiate the long-term status of American forces in the country.

---
